entities.summary:
Inflation is the sustained general increase in the price level of goods and services in an economy, resulting in a decrease in the purchasing power of money. Measured by indices such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and GDP deflator, inflation is one of the most fundamental macroeconomic phenomena — its causes, management, and consequences are central to monetary policy, central banking, and political economy.

Inflation was a persistent reality in pre-modern economies wherever currency debasement occurred — Roman emperors reduced silver content in denarii progressively, producing price inflation throughout the 3rd century CE. The Price Revolution of the 16th–17th centuries (significant European inflation attributed to New World silver inflows) transformed European economic life. Modern understanding of inflation developed through the 18th–20th centuries: David Hume's quantity theory of money, the bullionist controversy, 19th-century debates over the gold standard, and finally Keynes versus the monetarists (Milton Friedman's 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon').

The 20th century provided inflation's most dramatic case studies: German hyperinflation of 1921–1923 (a loaf of bread reaching 200 billion marks) destroyed the middle class and contributed to political radicalization that enabled Hitler. The stagflation of the 1970s (inflation + stagnation) destroyed the Keynesian consensus and brought monetarist policies and central bank independence to dominance. The post-2021 global inflation surge — caused by supply chain disruptions, energy shocks, and pandemic-era fiscal stimulus — tested central banks' credibility and triggered the fastest interest rate increases since the 1980s.
